newsitem.title: UK: British interest rates to rise and rise again.
newsitem.headline: British interest rates to rise and rise again.

text.p: A modest quarter-point rise in British interest rates is not enough to slow rampant consumer spending and is just one more step on a potentially long path of further monetary tightening, analysts said on Thursday.

Following a budget that did little to restrain consumer spending, they said the Bank of England's monetary policy committee might ultimately have to raise interest rates as high as eight percent from the new rate of 6.75. "The lack of measures to cool consumer demand in last week's budget didn't leave the Bank with much choice but to raise rates," said Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets. She forecast a further rate rise in August.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown tightened fiscal policy to the tune of nearly six billion pounds ($10 billion) in his first budget last week. But little of that was directed at the consumer and the corporate sector bore the brunt.
After raising rates on Thursday, the Bank of England said recent economic data had shown an upward revision to gross domestic product (GDP) growth and growing retail sales and money supply.
"That indicated a further tightening of monetary policy was necessary, notwithstanding the further appreciation of the exchange rate and the contractionary effects of the recent budget," it said.
Retail sales leapt 1.1 percent in May to stand more than five percent up year-on-year. The quarterly rate of growth was the highest since 1988, when Britain was in the grip of an unsustainable boom.
Overall, the economy grew by an annual 3.1 percent in the first quarter of the year, well above what economists see as a trend, or sustainable rate of growth, nearer two to 2.5 percent.
That growth is unlikely to abate soon as already spendthrift consumers get their hands on more than 30 billion pounds of free shares from mutually-owned building societies as they convert into banks.
"The UK consumer is doing very well and it will take a lot more than this (rate rise) to stop him," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist, Ciaran Barr.

He forecast base rates at 7.25 percent by the year-end, rising to eight percent in 1998. "The Bank will continue to be surprised by the strength of consumer demand. You have got to take those windfalls seriously. It runs the risk of responding to, not leading events."
But he said the strength of the pound -- up more than 20 percent in less than a year -- would make the central bank tread carefully for next month at least.

The Bank acknowledged it faces a worsening policy dilemma -- rampant consumer sales stand in stark contrast to a beleaguered manufacturing sector where exports have been ravaged by the super-strong pound.
Sterling dropped more than a pfennig after Thursday's rate rise as the currency market had hoped for a more aggressive policy tightening.

Strategists expect sterling to rise above three marks at any time, with German interest rates only three percent and Thursday's rate rise seen as merely one in a long line -- even though it is the third in as many months.
The pound stood at around 2.95 marks on Thursday afternoon.

Britain's top employers' organisation, the Confederation of British Industry, grudgingly recognised the need for a rate rise after Brown's budget, which it said did not do enough to slow domestic demand.
But it is hoping for the sake of manufacturers that no more increases are in the pipeline.

"We would stress that further interest rate rises in the short-term would be unwelcome," said CBI director-general, Adair Turner. The weakness of currencies pencilled in for European economic and monetary union and rate rises in Britain have already pushed sterling to levels that are hurting exporters badly.
"The situation should not be exacerbated and is itself likely to slow growth over the next year."

The Bank knows that further rate rises will do nothing to right the imbalance in the economy but it has to fulfil its mandate to control inflation. The inflationary threat comes clearly from consumers.
With little fiscal back-up from the chancellor and no budget due until next March, the Bank has little choice if it is to keep underlying inflation at 2.5 percent over the next two years.

But it might, in an ideal world, wait until the sting is taken out of sterling's rally. "Sterling has to crack at some point and it will be a deteriorating trade balance that will do it," Barr said. "That's when the Bank will really start tightening again." ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
